Name: aggregate_intent_reconstruction
Title: Blind to the Whole: LLMs Under-Integrate Decomposed Harm During Rollout, yet the Aggregate-Intent Direction Can Be Reconstructed and Re-Read
Short Hypothesis: Decomposition attacks succeed because, during ordinary turn-by-turn rollout, an aligned LLM computes per-subtask harmfulness but systematically UNDER-INTEGRATES it into a representation of the aggregate harmful goal that the benign-looking subtasks jointly serve. We separate known ingredients (decomposition attacks, linear harmful-intent probes, and external sequential monitors are all established) from four precise novel claims: (1) integration blindness -- the running-conversation harmfulness projection stays near-benign relative to the monolithic request, a gap we localize across layers and turns (represented-in-rollout vs reconstructable-off-rollout); (2) the aggregate-intent representation is dormant-not-absent -- a linear 'reconstructed-goal' direction is recoverable when the model is shown the accumulated conversation; (3) that reconstructed direction is causally sufficient enough that activation patching into a decomposed run restores refusal; and (4) a training-free 'intent-integration probe' (IIP) that re-reads cumulative context onto this direction each turn detects emerging cumulative harm before the final step, giving an internal, white-box alternative to external plan-level monitors. We state the integration claim as graded (under-integration relative to monolithic prompts), not absolute.
Related Work: Known ingredients we build on, and do not claim as novel: (i) decomposition/compositional attacks -- 'Adversaries Can Misuse Combinations of Safe Models' (2024), 'Safe in Isolation, Dangerous Together' (2025), STAC (2025), CKA-Agent (2025), Semantic Intent Fragmentation (2026) -- all report >90% attack success by splitting a harmful goal into benign subtasks; (ii) linear harmful-intent probing on residual streams; and (iii) EXTERNAL defenses -- lightweight sequential LLM monitors ('Monitoring Decomposition Attacks', 2025) and plan-level judges / information-flow taint (SIF's Compositional Intent Verifier, 2026). Mechanistically, 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows models encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST. Our delta is three-fold and distinct from each closest family. (1) Against external cumulative-context monitors: they add a separate judge over the transcript; we ask whether the TARGET model's OWN state represents aggregate intent during normal rollout, and show it under-integrates rather than being read by an outside observer. (2) Against harmful-intent linear-recoverability papers: recovering intent from a full concatenated prompt does not imply the model fails to integrate WHILE it is generating decomposed turns -- we separate represented-in-rollout from reconstructable-off-rollout and localize where integration fails across layers/turns. (3) We extend 'Expected Harm' from severity/cost to the cumulative-goal dimension, add a causal patching test, and deliver a training-free internal probe compared head-to-head against the external monitors at matched context and latency.
Abstract: Large language models refuse overtly harmful requests yet are trivially defeated by decomposition attacks that split a harmful goal into individually benign subtasks -- attack success often exceeds 90%, and the setting is increasingly load-bearing for multi-turn assistants, tool-using agents, and long-horizon copilots. Existing defenses bolt an external monitor or plan-level judge onto the system. We instead ask a mechanistic question: during ordinary rollout, does the model itself internally represent the aggregate harmful goal that its benign subtasks jointly serve? We hypothesize it systematically under-integrates -- computing per-subtask harmfulness but not the integrated goal -- and that this dormant-but-recoverable 'aggregate intent' is the crux of decomposition blindness. We test this in three parts. First, using paired data (a monolithic harmful request vs. its benign decomposition), we extract a linear harmfulness direction and show its projection is high for the monolithic request but collapses to near-benign for each decomposed subtask and for the running conversation processed turn-by-turn, and we localize the integration gap across layers and turns. Second, we show the aggregate goal is latent: feeding the model the concatenated conversation and prompting it to infer the overall objective recovers a 'reconstructed-goal' direction whose projection re-separates harmful from benign decompositions, and activation patching this component into a decomposed run causally restores refusal. Third, we build Intent-Integration Probing (IIP), a training-free defense that at each turn re-reads cumulative context onto the reconstructed-goal direction to flag emerging cumulative harm. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we report detection lead-time, decomposition-attack defense success, over-refusal, utility, and per-turn compute, comparing IIP against external sequential monitors. If the result is negative -- if strong nonlinear probes decode aggregate intent during rollout, or patching does not selectively restore refusal -- that is itself decision-relevant: it argues external monitors are necessary because the signal already exists internally, and we report it as such.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment except the LoRA reference in Experiment 4. All "directions" are difference-in-means vectors on residual-stream activations; all "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Every reported number is averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) governing data sampling, attacker-LLM generation, and steering noise; we report mean and a 95% bootstrap CI. Everything fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: 400 harmful behaviors from HarmBench and 313 from StrongREJECT (713 monolithic harmful requests). For each we generate a benign multi-subtask decomposition with an attacker LLM (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, temperature 0.7, the Safe-in-Isolation/CKA-Agent recipe: 3-6 individually-benign subtasks that jointly reconstruct the goal). We keep the 500 decompositions (of 713) that pass a two-judge screen (every subtask judged benign in isolation by Llama-Guard-3; the whole chain judged to reconstruct the original goal by GPT-4o-mini) and cap at 500 to bound attacker-API cost. Negatives: 500 genuinely-benign multi-step conversations matched on turn count and length, drawn from ShareGPT multi-turn logs filtered benign. Split 300/100/100 train/val/test by goal, no goal crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - integration blindness): Tests whether the model computes per-subtask harmfulness but never forms an internal representation of the aggregated goal. Decisive metric: the integration gap G = proj_harm(monolithic request) - max over turns t of proj_harm(running conversation at turn t), expressed in units of the pooled within-class SD of the harmfulness projection. Data: the 500 decompositions plus 500 benign negatives. Model: the three frozen models; harmfulness direction from difference-in-means on 300 monolithic-harmful vs 300 harmless training requests at the last prompt token, layer picked on val by probe AUROC. We record proj_harm for (a) the monolithic request, (b) each subtask in isolation, (c) the running conversation processed turn-by-turn (last token at each turn). Convincing: mean G >= 1.5 SD, with (b) and (c) statistically indistinguishable from the benign-negative distribution (two-sided t, p>0.05) while (a) sits >= 3 SD above it, on all three models. Indecision band: G in [0.5, 1.5] SD - the representation is partially integrated, so "never forms" is downgraded to "under-forms" and H2/H3 are reframed as amplifying a weak signal rather than reconstructing an absent one; we commit to that reframing now. Negative (G < 0.5 SD, running projection tracks the monolithic one): the model does integrate, refuting H1; decomposition then succeeds for some other reason, which we report without proceeding to the H3 defense.

Experiment 2 (H2 - dormant-but-recoverable aggregate-intent direction): Tests that the aggregate goal is latent (essentially absent under decomposition), recoverable as a linear direction from the concatenated context, and causally sufficient to restore refusal. Decisive metric: test-set AUROC of the reconstructed-goal projection separating harmful from benign decompositions, read against the raw running-projection AUROC of Experiment 1. Data: the same 500/500, test split (100/100). Procedure: feed each frozen model its own concatenated conversation and prompt it to state the overall objective; extract a reconstructed-goal direction by difference-in-means on activations for inferred-harmful vs inferred-benign objectives (train split); read its projection on test. Causal leg: activation patching that injects the reconstructed-goal component into a decomposed run at the final-subtask decision token, scoring refusal-restoration rate (fraction of previously-complied harmful decompositions now judge-scored as refused), against two controls (patch a benign-goal component; patch a random norm-matched direction). Convincing: reconstructed AUROC >= 0.80 while raw running AUROC <= 0.65 (a >= 0.15 gap), AND patching restores refusal on >= 40% of cases versus <= 5% for both controls. Indecision band: reconstructed AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] OR restoration in [15%, 40%] - the direction carries partial but not decisive aggregate intent; H2 is supported only as "partially recoverable" and we report the recovery ceiling. Negative (reconstructed AUROC <= 0.65 or restoration within 15 points of controls): the aggregate goal is not linearly recoverable or not causally sufficient, refuting H2 and predicting the H3 defense will fail.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Intent-Integration Probing detects cumulative harm before completion and improves on external monitors): Tests that a training-free per-turn re-read of the reconstructed-goal projection flags emerging cumulative harm before the final step, with a better lead-time / defense / over-refusal trade-off than external monitors. Decisive metric: mean detection lead-time L = number of subtasks before the final harmful subtask at which the alarm first fires on true-positive attacks, reported jointly with decomposition-attack defense success and benign over-refusal. Data: held-out test attacks from three families (Safe-in-Isolation-style, STAC-style, CKA-style; ~100 each, generated as above on a disjoint goal set), the 100 benign multi-step test negatives, XSTest (450 prompts) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample for over-refusal, and MT-Bench (80) plus a 2,000-question MMLU subsample for utility. IIP: at each turn run the goal-reconstruction read and threshold the reconstructed-goal projection; threshold fixed on val at 1% FPR against benign negatives. Systems compared (decisive metric first, then defense success, then over-refusal): IIP vs (i) a per-turn harmfulness probe with no integration, (ii) Llama-Guard-3 per turn, (iii) a lightweight external sequential LLM monitor (Qwen2.5-7B judge, Monitoring-Decomposition-Attacks style), (iv) a plan-level LLM judge. Convincing: IIP fires >= 2 subtasks before completion on >= 60% of true positives AND lands within 5 points of the best external monitor on defense success while its over-refusal on benign multi-step negatives is >= 10 points lower than that monitor. Indecision band: lead-time in [1, 2) subtasks OR defense-success gap to the best monitor in [5, 15] points - IIP is a viable cheaper white-box option but not clearly early or dominant, and we report it as complementary. Negative (lead-time < 1, i.e., fires only at/after the final step, or over-refusal no better than the monitors): IIP offers no early-warning or trade-off gain and we report external monitoring as preferable. We log forward passes per turn so the reviewer sees IIP adds one reconstruction pass rather than a full separate monitor call.

Experiment 4 (H2/H3 robustness and adaptive cost): Tests whether the reconstructed-goal direction transfers across attack and model families and how much an adaptive attacker must pay to evade it. Decisive metric: cross-family transfer AUROC (direction extracted on one attack family, evaluated on another) and the multiplicative increase in subtask count an adaptive attacker needs to push IIP below 1% TPR at 1% FPR. Data: the three attack families above; adaptive attacker = the same attacker LLM instructed to maximize pairwise semantic distance between subtasks (target embedding cosine < 0.3). Model: the frozen models, plus one reference point of a 20-step LoRA-tuned probe (rank 8, lr 1e-4, one seed) to check whether light tuning beats the training-free read. Convincing: transfer AUROC drops by <= 0.10 across families AND the adaptive attacker needs >= 2x more subtasks (raising its own detectability and cost) to evade. Indecision band: transfer drop in [0.10, 0.20] - the direction is family-specific and must be re-extracted per family, which we state. Negative (transfer drop > 0.20, or adaptive evasion at no extra subtask cost): the mechanism is brittle and we scope the claim to non-adaptive, in-family decomposition.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Goal reconstruction relies on the model's own inference; if the model cannot infer the aggregate goal even when shown the full conversation, the reconstructed-goal direction will be weak — this is itself an informative negative but limits the defense. 2) The integration gap may be partial rather than binary; some models may re-integrate somewhat, weakening the 'blindness' claim. 3) Reconstruction adds an extra forward pass per turn (cost), though still cheaper than a separate large monitor. 4) Benign multi-step conversations that plausibly infer to a harmful goal could cause over-refusal; the benign-negatives set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single harmfulness/goal direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 6) Adaptive attackers maximizing subtask semantic dispersion may evade reconstruction, though this constrains the attack and raises cost. 7) Directions and thresholds are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated decompositions.

Name: irreversibility_blind_agent_safety
Title: Consequence Without a Compass: LLMs Encode Content Harm but Weakly Encode Action Irreversibility, and Re-Injecting It Narrows the Text-Action Safety Gap
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request's CONTENT is harmful, but have a weak-or-absent internal representation of whether a tool CALL is IRREVERSIBLE / high-consequence (deleting a database, wiring money, or sending an email cannot be undone; reading a file can). We define irreversibility precisely as a property of the action's real-world effect -- distinct from content harm (is the topic dangerous?), from severity (how bad is the harm?), and from execution cost -- namely, whether the effect can be rolled back. We hypothesize this missing irreversibility representation is A mechanistic cause (not necessarily the sole cause) of the text-safety-does-not-transfer-to-tool-call-safety gap: because refusal is gated on content harm alone, an agent will execute an irreversible destructive action whenever the surface content looks benign. We further hypothesize the irreversibility signal is latent-but-recoverable (a linear direction emerges when the model is prompted to reason about consequences) and can be re-injected at the tool-call decision point to condition refusal on consequence, narrowing the gap without hurting benign tool use. The scientific contribution (irreversibility as a distinct, causally-tested latent axis) and the practical contribution (a training-free re-injection defense) are separable and each stands on its own.
Related Work: Known ingredients: the GAP benchmark ('Mind the GAP', 2026) shows text-level refusal does not transfer to tool-call safety across six frontier models but is purely black-box; SafeKeep ('Tool Specifications Matter', 2026) locates ONE cause -- schema-formatted tool specs weaken internal refusal -- and decouples judgment from execution via flattened specs; 'Read the Scene, Not the Script' (2025) defines 'consequence-blindness' behaviorally and fixes it with consequence-reasoning fine-tuning; 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows via linear probing that models encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST; AgentTrust/CIP/Thought-Aligner are external monitors or CoT correctors. Our delta: (1) we advance and CAUSALLY test a specific missing internal object -- an action-irreversibility representation, sharply distinguished above from content harm, severity, and execution cost -- as A mechanistic root of the text-action gap, rather than attributing it to schema format (SafeKeep) or treating consequence-blindness only behaviorally (Read-the-Scene). Irreversibility is not a relabeling of consequence-blindness: consequence-blindness is a behavioral failure to reason about outcomes, whereas we test a specific, linearly-readable axis (roll-back-able vs not) that dissociates from content harm and is separately steerable. (2) We extend Expected-Harm's cost-blindness from severity to the actionable irreversibility axis in the AGENTIC tool-call setting and show it is dormant-not-missing. (3) We build a training-free irreversibility re-injection defense at the tool-call boundary and compare directly to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors, verifying schema-flattening alone does not recover the raw irreversibility signal (distinct mechanisms).
Abstract: LLM agents refuse harmful requests in text yet still execute the corresponding harmful tool calls -- text safety does not transfer to action safety, and in deployed agents a single wrongly-executed irreversible call (dropping a production table, wiring funds, mass-sending an email) is operationally far costlier than a wrong sentence. We propose a mechanistic explanation: aligned LLMs encode whether a request's CONTENT is harmful but lack a robust internal representation of whether an ACTION is IRREVERSIBLE -- whether its real-world effect can be rolled back -- an axis we distinguish from content harm, severity, and execution cost. Because refusal is gated on content harm, agents comply with destructive-but-innocuous-looking actions. We test this on open-weights tool-using models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Ministral-8B). First, using paired tool calls that hold content roughly fixed while flipping reversibility (read vs. delete, draft vs. send, simulate vs. execute), we extract a content-harm direction and a candidate irreversibility direction and test whether activations separate reversible from irreversible calls, expecting content harm to be linearly readable but irreversibility weak and near-orthogonal to it. Second, we show irreversibility is dormant-not-absent: prompting the model to reason about consequences recovers a 'reconstructed-consequence' direction that re-separates the pairs, and activation patching it into a blind run restores refusal on irreversible calls (with content-harm-only and random controls to show specificity). Third, we build Irreversibility Re-Injection (IRI), a training-free intervention that reads/re-injects the consequence direction at the tool-call decision token. We evaluate on the GAP benchmark and a reversibility-labeled tool suite, measuring the text-action gap, harmful-call blocking, benign tool-use utility, and over-refusal, comparing IRI to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors. If the hypothesis is false -- irreversibility already well-encoded, or patching non-specific -- we learn the gap lies elsewhere (e.g., schema format) and report which practices (gating, monitoring, prompt design, fine-tuning) that redirects.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and Ministral-8B-Instruct (8-14B-parameter tool-using instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment (no fine-tuning anywhere). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) controlling data sampling and steering noise; we report mean and 95% bootstrap CI. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - a reversibility-labeled tool suite of 400 minimal pairs on two orthogonal axes, content-harm (harmful/benign) and reversibility (reversible/irreversible), holding content roughly fixed while flipping reversibility (read_file vs delete_file, draft_email vs send_email, query_db vs drop_table, simulate vs execute): 100 pairs each across pharma, finance, infrastructure, and file-ops, sourced from GAP-benchmark scenarios, ToolEmu/InjecAgent tool schemas, and hand-built pairs. Reversibility labels are set by two authors on clear cases only and spot-checked by a third rater (report Cohen's kappa; discard pairs with kappa-level disagreement). Split 200/100/100 pairs train/val/test with no tool crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - content harm is readable, irreversibility is not): Tests whether the models linearly encode content harm but weakly encode action irreversibility, and that the two axes are near-orthogonal. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC of the raw irreversibility direction separating irreversible from reversible calls, contrasted with the content-harm AUROC; secondary metric the absolute cosine between the two directions. Data: the 400-pair suite (200 train / 100 test). Model: the four frozen models; content-harm direction from difference-in-means on harmful vs benign requests and a candidate irreversibility direction from difference-in-means on irreversible vs reversible calls, both at the tool-call decision token, layer chosen on val by content-harm probe AUROC. Convincing: content-harm AUROC >= 0.85 while raw irreversibility AUROC <= 0.65 and |cosine| <= 0.20, on at least three of four models (the "blindness" signature). Indecision band: raw irreversibility AUROC in [0.65, 0.75] - irreversibility is weakly but non-trivially encoded, so we recast the claim as "under-represented" rather than "absent" and carry that wording into H2/H4. Negative (raw irreversibility AUROC >= 0.75): the model already encodes irreversibility well, refuting H1; this is an informative, publishable negative and we report it rather than proceeding to the re-injection defense.

Experiment 2 (H3 - irreversibility is dormant-not-absent, recoverable by consequence reasoning): Tests that prompting the model to reason about action consequences recovers a linear consequence direction that separates the pairs the raw signal could not. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the reconstructed-consequence projection separating irreversible from reversible calls, read against the raw irreversibility AUROC of Experiment 1. Data: the same suite, test split. Procedure: prompt each frozen model to reason explicitly about consequences before deciding; extract a reconstructed-consequence direction by difference-in-means on activations for inferred-irreversible vs inferred-reversible (train split); read its projection on test. Convincing: reconstructed AUROC >= 0.80 and at least 0.15 above the raw irreversibility AUROC, on at least three of four models. Indecision band: reconstructed AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] or an improvement over raw of [0.05, 0.15] - irreversibility is only partly recoverable and we report the ceiling, tempering H4's expected gains. Negative (reconstructed AUROC <= 0.65 or no improvement over raw): the model cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, refuting H3 and predicting the H4 defense will be limited; we report this.

Experiment 3 (H2 - the missing irreversibility representation causally drives the text-action gap): Tests that re-injecting the consequence component restores refusal on irreversible-but-innocuous-looking calls, whereas content-harm alone does not. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate = fraction of previously-executed irreversible-benign-looking calls now refused or gated (judge-scored) after patching the reconstructed-consequence component, against controls. Data: the harmful/irreversible and benign/irreversible test cells (~50 calls). Procedure: (a) patch the reconstructed-consequence component from a consequence-reasoning run into a schema-only "blind" run; (b) control - patch content-harm alone (expected little effect on destructive-but-benign-looking calls); (c) reverse - patch a reversible-consequence component into an irreversible run and measure induced compliance; plus a random norm-matched direction control. Convincing: consequence-patching restores refusal/gating on >= 40% of cases while content-harm-only and random controls stay <= 10%, and the reverse patch raises compliance on irreversible calls by >= 20 points. Indecision band: consequence-patching restoration in [15%, 40%] above controls - irreversibility is one contributing cause but not the sole bottleneck, and we say so before running. Negative (restoration within 15 points of controls): irreversibility is not the causal cause of the gap, refuting H2; we would then attribute the gap elsewhere (e.g., schema format) and report it.

Experiment 4 (H4 - Irreversibility Re-Injection closes the gap without hurting benign tool use and stacks with schema-flattening): Tests that reading and re-injecting the consequence direction at the tool-call token closes the text-action gap while preserving benign tool use, and is complementary to schema-flattening. Decisive metric: the text-action safety gap = (harmful-tool-call execution rate) - (harmful-text compliance rate), reported jointly with benign tool-use utility and over-refusal. Data: the GAP benchmark plus our suite for the gap and harmful-call blocking; ToolBench and API-Bank for benign tool-use utility (report task success on a fixed 500-call subsample each); benign-irreversible legitimate calls (should not be blanket-blocked, ideally confirmation-prompted); benign-reversible calls and XSTest (450) for over-refusal. IRI: at the tool-call decision token compute the reconstructed-consequence projection and, when it indicates high irreversibility, add an activation nudge re-inflating the consequence signal (one fixed strength per model, tuned on val). Systems compared (decisive metric first): IRI vs no defense, SafeKeep schema-flattening, an external Llama-Guard/AgentTrust-style monitor, content-harm-direction-only steering, and IRI+SafeKeep stacked; we also verify schema-flattening alone does NOT recover the raw irreversibility AUROC of Experiment 1 (to show the two causes are distinct). Convincing: IRI cuts the text-action gap by >= 50% relative to no-defense, blocks >= 80% of harmful-irreversible calls, keeps benign-reversible over-refusal within 5 points of no-defense and benign tool-use utility within 3 points, and Pareto-dominates content-only steering; and IRI+SafeKeep improves on either alone (stacking). Indecision band: gap reduction in [20%, 50%] or benign-utility loss in [3, 8] points - IRI helps but at a usability cost we report on the Pareto curve rather than claiming a clean closure. Negative (gap reduction < 20% or benign-utility loss > 8 points, or IRI no better than content-only steering): re-injection does not close the gap cheaply, refuting H4; we report the limit. Adaptive check: an attacker who phrases irreversible actions to look maximally reversible; we report whether IRI still fires and whether the required disguise raises attack cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Irreversibility may be partly entangled with content-harm rather than a clean separate axis; if so the decomposition weakens — the orthogonality and patching experiments directly test this. 2) The model may already encode irreversibility better than hypothesized (raw AUROC high), which would refute the blindness claim but is itself an informative, publishable negative result. 3) Reconstruction depends on the model's own consequence-reasoning; if it cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, the recovered direction is weak and IRI is limited. 4) Legitimate benign-but-irreversible actions (a user genuinely wanting to send an email or delete a file) risk being over-blocked; we target confirmation-gating rather than blanket refusal and quantify this via the benign-irreversible utility set and Pareto sweep. 5) A single consequence direction may be multi-dimensional (severity vs irreversibility vs scope), requiring subspace projection. 6) Building faithful reversibility labels is subjective for some tools; we restrict to clear cases and spot-check with human raters. 7) Directions and re-injection strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results are on open-weights agents and may not directly transfer to closed API agents.

Name: cross_lingual_belief_action_gap
Title: Does It Not Understand, or Just Not Refuse? Disentangling Comprehension Failure from Action Failure in Cross-Lingual Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Our central question is: are low-resource-language jailbreaks primarily BELIEF failures, ACTION failures, or a tier-dependent mixture? When a harmful request is posed in a low-resource language, the model's failure to refuse could stem from two mechanistically opposite causes: (A) a COMPREHENSION failure, where the internal harmfulness BELIEF is absent/degraded because the model does not deeply represent the request, or (B) an ACTION failure, where the belief is preserved but the refusal action is not triggered. We operationalize 'harmfulness belief present' as: the model's activation projection onto a language-shared harmfulness-belief direction is at or above the harmful-class threshold set on a held-out English calibration set. We hypothesize these two modes are separable, that their balance shifts systematically with language-resource tier (action failures dominate at high/mid resource, comprehension failures rise at the lowest tier), and that whichever dominates dictates which defense works -- belief re-coupling where belief is preserved, belief reconstruction where it is absent -- a distinction prior multilingual-safety work has not made because it measured only the refusal direction, never the harmfulness-belief direction.
Related Work: Prior multilingual-safety mechanistic work measures the REFUSAL side only. 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (2025) and Minionese (2026) show low-resource jailbreaks leave 'the refusal mechanism intact but untriggered'; SS-Neuron (2026) and Soteria (2025) locate/tune cross-lingual safety neurons/heads; OmniGuard (2025) builds an external language-agnostic harmful-prompt classifier; 'The Hidden Space of Safety' (2025) shows weaker safe/unsafe separation in non-English. Crucially, these either treat safety as a single refusal signal or build an external classifier, and none disentangle the model's internal harmfulness BELIEF from its refusal ACTION per language. Zhao et al. (2025) separated belief from action but only in English. Our contribution imports the belief/action decomposition into the cross-lingual setting to answer the question the field assumed away -- is a low-resource jailbreak a comprehension failure (belief absent) or an action failure (belief present, refusal untriggered)? -- introduces a NEW object, a cross-lingual harmfulness-BELIEF direction (not another refusal probe), shows the failure mix is tier-dependent, and derives a defense whose per-language success is PREDICTED by which failure mode dominates. This matters operationally because refusal-steering defenses, which assume belief is present, may be systematically miscalibrated for non-English users.
Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs is notoriously brittle across languages: a request refused in English is often answered when translated into a low-resource language. The prevailing mechanistic account says the model still 'knows' the request is harmful but its refusal is simply not triggered. We argue this is incomplete because it measures only the refusal signal and never asks whether the model's internal harmfulness BELIEF survives translation. We disentangle two opposite failure modes: a comprehension failure (the harmfulness belief itself is degraded) versus an action failure (the belief is intact but refusal is not engaged), where 'belief present' means the projection onto a language-shared harmfulness-belief direction meets the harmful-class threshold. Building on the belief/action decomposition, we extract a language-shared harmfulness-belief direction and a refusal-action direction and measure both across resource-tiered languages and perturbation types (translation, transliteration, code-switching), with explicit controls for general language competence, translation quality, and semantic preservation so a low belief projection is not merely poor embeddings. Our central hypothesis is that the balance of failure modes shifts with tier -- high/mid-resource jailbreaks are mostly action failures, the lowest-resource ones increasingly comprehension failures -- and that this predicts which defense works: belief re-coupling helps only where belief is preserved, whereas belief must first be reconstructed where it is absent (plainly: if belief is absent, steering won't help; if present, recoupling should). We validate causally via activation patching (patch the English belief component into a non-English run) and evaluate training-free belief-recoupling and belief-reconstruction defenses on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B across tiers, reporting attack-success reduction, over-refusal, and utility against refusal-direction steering and external multilingual guards. The result gives red-teamers, safety teams, model builders, and multilingual evaluators a diagnosis-first tool rather than a claim of universal multilingual safety.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter multilingual instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment (no fine-tuning; the SS-Neuron baseline in Experiment 4 tunes only its own reported neuron set). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: 300 harmful and 300 benign base prompts (harmful from MultiJail/PolyRefuse pools, benign from translated XSTest/OR-Bench), each rendered across a resource-tiered language set - high (English, Chinese, German), mid (Hindi, Vietnamese), low (Zulu, Scots-Gaelic, Yoruba) - and three perturbation types (clean translation, transliteration, code-switching). Translations reuse existing MultiJail/PolyRefuse/Minionese-style data where available and are otherwise machine-translated then spot-checked by native/fluent raters on a 10% sample per language (report adequacy pass rate; drop languages below 80% adequacy). Split base prompts 150/75/75 train/val/test, no prompt crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - belief and action are separable and the two failure modes are distinguishable): Tests that a harmfulness-belief direction and a refusal-action direction can be extracted, are distinct, and that per-(language, prompt) states fall into separable action-failure vs comprehension-failure clusters. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of a two-way classifier (action-failure = belief high + refusal low vs comprehension-failure = belief low + refusal low) using the two projections as features. Secondary: cosine between the belief and refusal directions (should be well below 1, showing they are not the same axis). Data: the tiered set, test split. Model: three frozen models; belief direction from difference-in-means on harmful vs harmless prompts at the last instruction token, refusal direction from difference-in-means at the last post-instruction token; each extracted English-only and language-shared (mean over the high/mid safety-aligned languages), each validated by held-out probe AUROC and single-language causal steering. Convincing: the failure-mode classifier reaches AUROC >= 0.80 and the belief/refusal cosine <= 0.5, on all three models. Indecision band: classifier AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] - the two failure modes overlap and coexist within prompts, so the tier trend in H2 is reported as a soft gradient rather than a partition. Negative (classifier AUROC <= 0.65 or belief/refusal cosine > 0.8): belief and action are not separable in the cross-lingual setting, refuting H1 and collapsing the study to the existing single-refusal-direction account, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the failure-mode balance shifts with resource tier): Tests that comprehension failures rise and action failures fall as resource tier drops. Decisive metric: the slope of the comprehension-failure fraction versus resource tier (ordinal high>mid>low), tested for a monotone increase (Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test). Secondary: a belief-preservation curve (mean belief projection vs tier) and the correlation between per-language belief-projection drop and attack-success rate. Data: the full tiered/perturbed set, test split, judged for attack success (Llama-Guard-3 plus a StrongREJECT-style rubric, verified where checkable). Model: the three frozen models with directions from Experiment 1. Convincing: comprehension-failure fraction increases monotonically with a significant trend (p<0.05) on all three models, and belief-drop correlates with attack-success at Spearman rho >= 0.5. Indecision band: a positive but non-significant trend, or rho in [0.3, 0.5] - the tier effect is suggestive, and we report it as a weak dependence rather than a systematic shift. Negative (flat or reversed trend, rho < 0.3): the failure mix does not track tier, refuting H2; low-resource jailbreaks would then be a single failure mode across tiers, which we report. We separately confirm belief-drop and refusal-drop dissociate (differ in tier profile) to rule out a single collapsing signal.

Experiment 3 (H3 - the dominant failure mode predicts and is causally validated by which defense works): Tests, causally, that patching the English/language-shared belief component restores refusal for action-failures but not comprehension-failures, and behaviorally that belief-recoupling helps where belief is preserved while belief-reconstruction is needed where it is absent. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate under belief-patching, split by failure mode (action-failure vs comprehension-failure), with the prediction that restoration is high for the former and low for the latter. Data: test-split harmful (language, prompt) states pre-classified into failure modes by Experiment 1. Procedure: (a) patch the language-shared belief component into a non-English run and score restored refusal; (b) control - patch the refusal-action component alone; (c) random norm-matched control. Convincing: restoration >= 40% for action-failures and <= 15% for comprehension-failures (a >= 25-point split), with the refusal-only and random controls near zero on action-failures relative to belief-patching. Indecision band: the action-minus-comprehension restoration split in [10, 25] points - belief-patching helps somewhat regardless of mode, so the diagnostic is partially but not sharply predictive, which we report. Negative (split < 10 points): restoration does not depend on failure mode, refuting the causal dichotomy in H3; the belief/action framing would then not guide defense choice, which we report.

Experiment 4 (H3 defense - belief-recoupling vs belief-reconstruction, per tier): Tests that the failure-mode diagnostic predicts which training-free defense wins per language. Decisive metric: attack-success rate after defense on tiered/perturbed harmful test sets, reported jointly with over-refusal and utility, and compared against the diagnostic's per-language prediction of which defense should win. Data: tiered harmful test sets (attack success judged as above); tiered benign sets (translated XSTest/OR-Bench, plus code-switched benign) for over-refusal; tiered MMLU (2,000-question subsample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Defenses: belief-recoupling (read belief projection; where belief is preserved but refusal untriggered, nudge belief into the refusal pathway) and a belief-reconstruction variant (first anchor belief with the language-shared belief prototype, then recouple), each at one fixed strength per model per tier tuned on val. Systems compared (decisive metric first): the two defenses vs no defense, English refusal-direction steering, language-shared refusal steering, an OmniGuard-style external guard, and SS-Neuron tuning. Convincing: at high/mid tier belief-recoupling Pareto-dominates refusal-only steering (>= 15-point larger attack-success reduction at equal or lower over-refusal), while at the lowest tier belief-reconstruction is needed and beats recoupling by >= 10 points - and the failure-mode diagnostic from Experiment 2 correctly predicts the winning defense for >= 70% of languages. Indecision band: diagnostic prediction accuracy in [55%, 70%] or defense gaps in [5, 10] points - the diagnostic is informative but not decisive, which we report. Negative (diagnostic prediction <= 55% or no defense separation by tier): failure mode does not predict the winning defense, refuting the practical payoff of H3; we report that a single defense suffices or that neither works at the lowest tier. Adaptive check: an attacker choosing the language that maximally degrades belief; we report whether this raises attack cost or fluency loss.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Belief and comprehension may not be cleanly separable from generic representation quality in low-resource languages; a low belief projection could reflect poor embeddings generally rather than a specific harmfulness-belief deficit — the harmless-control projections and patching experiments help disentangle this. 2) The two failure modes may coexist within a single prompt rather than cleanly partitioning, blurring the tier trend. 3) A single belief direction may be multi-dimensional or not parallel across very distant languages, weakening the language-shared prototype; subspace projection may be needed. 4) Belief reconstruction for comprehension-failure cases may be unreliable if the model genuinely cannot represent the request's meaning, limiting the low-tier defense (itself an informative negative). 5) Translation-quality artifacts could confound belief measurements; we mitigate with native/spot-checked data but cannot fully eliminate. 6) Directions, nudge strengths, and thresholds are model- and language-specific and require calibration. 7) Results depend on available low-resource benchmarks, which are sparse and English-translation-derived, potentially missing culturally-rooted harms.

Name: hidden_completion_refusal_fragility
Title: Not All Refusals Are Equal: Refusals That Secretly Compute the Harmful Answer Are the Fragile Ones
Short Hypothesis: A safety-aligned LLM can emit an identical-looking refusal for two mechanistically opposite reasons: (A) a shallow refusal where it never internally computes the harmful content, or (B) a concealed-completion refusal where it fully computes and internally represents the harmful answer and merely gates it at the output boundary. The known facts we build on are that refusals can hide unsafe internal content and that refusals can be brittle; what is NEW is a graded, operationally-defined 'harmful-completion depth' axis -- how much of the specific harmful answer is linearly decodable from activations at the refusal point -- and the CAUSAL claim that this depth predicts fragility. We hypothesize depth is (1) linearly readable from activations, and (2) causally predicts a refusal's FRAGILITY: concealed-completion refusals are far more easily broken by prefill, refusal-cliff-head ablation, or lightweight fine-tuning than shallow refusals, because the harmful knowledge is already present and only weakly suppressed. We pre-register that depth need not track every attack equally (e.g., prefill should exploit depth strongly, abliteration may break refusals regardless).
Related Work: Prior work documents that refusals can hide unsafe internal content but does not stratify refusals by fragility. 'CoT is Not the Chain of Truth' (2026) and Beyond-Safe-Answers/BSA (2025) show 'superficial safety alignment' -- safe outputs while internal reasoning propagates unsafe narratives -- but treat this as a uniform, descriptive property. 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) shows refusal collapses at final tokens via suppression heads, and 'Adversarial Manipulation using Internal Representations' (2025) finds a caution direction in CoT, but neither asks whether different refusals differ in how much harmful content was internally computed, nor links that to attack fragility. Our delta is narrow and sharp: (1) we introduce a graded, decodability-based 'harmful-completion depth' scalar behind refusals -- explicitly more than 'the model knows the topic': it measures whether the specific harmful ANSWER is linearly decodable at the refusal point, and we include negative controls (harmful-but-no-refusal prompts, refusal-but-no-harm-computation prompts, matched length/format) to show it is not mere harmfulness recognition or prompt difficulty; (2) we advance and causally test that depth predicts fragility, turning refusal into a two-class object (robust vs brittle); and (3) we derive a fragility-auditing metric and a Completion-Suppression training signal that reshapes brittle concealed-completion refusals into shallow non-engagement refusals -- neither of which prior work targets. Operationally this gives labs a release-audit and red-team-prioritization tool: two models with identical refusal RATES can differ sharply in how many of those refusals are brittle.
Abstract: Safety evaluations treat a refusal as a success. We argue this hides a critical distinction: two refusals identical in text can be mechanistically opposite. In a shallow refusal the model never internally computes the harmful content; in a concealed-completion refusal it fully computes and internally represents the harmful answer, then suppresses it only at the output boundary. The latter is dangerous precisely because the harmful knowledge is present and only lightly gated, so a small perturbation exposes it. We define 'completion depth' operationally as the degree to which the specific harmful answer is linearly decodable from activations at the refusal point, and hypothesize it is linearly readable and causally predicts a refusal's fragility. We test this on open-weights models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and reasoning models DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, s1.1). First, we build prompts that elicit refusals with controllably different completion depth (direct vs. educational-framing vs. decomposed) and read depth by probing whether the harmful answer is linearly decodable despite the refusal, against negative controls that rule out generic harmfulness recognition. Second, we causally test fragility as a function of measured depth under prefill, refusal-cliff-head ablation, and 20-step benign fine-tuning, pre-registering which attacks should and should not track depth, and use activation patching to show injecting the depth component makes a shallow refusal brittle. Third, we package the depth measure as a 'refusal fragility audit' that flags which held-out refusals will break, and introduce a Completion-Suppression fine-tuning objective that converts brittle refusals into robust shallow ones. We report completion-depth AUROC, fragility prediction, and post-training attack-success reduction versus utility and over-refusal. We include an end-to-end use case: two models with matched refusal rates that the audit shows are meaningfully different, changing which model a lab would ship.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and the reasoning models DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and s1.1 (8B-parameter instruction/reasoning decoders). All weights are frozen except in Experiment 4, which LoRA-fine-tunes. "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations; a "decodability probe" is a linear read of the harmful answer from internal states. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling, attack randomness, and fine-tuning; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: harmful goals that all yield a textual refusal, from HarmBench (400 behaviors) and StrongREJECT (313 prompts), of which we keep the ~500 that produce a surface refusal on all four models (capping to bound compute). Each goal is elicited under four conditions expected to induce different internal completion depth: (a) direct harmful request (expect shallow), (b) educational/Malicious-Educator framing (expect deep concealed completion), (c) decomposed/roleplay framing, (d) for the reasoning models, a chain-of-thought rollout that may fully compute the answer before a final refusal. Split goals 300/100/100 train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - completion depth behind a refusal is linearly readable): Tests that the depth of internal harmful computation at a refusal is readable from activations, i.e. that identical-looking refusals differ measurably in internal depth. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the harmful-answer decodability probe (can the key harmful facts / first-harmful-token distribution be linearly read from activations at the refusal point), reported per condition (a)-(d). Secondary: the projection onto a harmful-content direction (difference-in-means on activations where the model does vs does not internally produce harmful content). Data: the ~500 goals x four conditions, test split. Model: the four frozen models; probe/direction fit on train, layer chosen on val by decodability AUROC; for reasoning models we additionally read depth across CoT tokens. Convincing: decodability AUROC >= 0.80 on held-out prompts AND the depth measure separates the conditions with the predicted ordering (educational > decomposed > direct; CoT high for reasoning models), consistent on at least three of four models. Indecision band: decodability AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] - depth is partially readable, and we report it as a noisy graded signal that weakens but does not void the fragility test. Negative (decodability AUROC <= 0.65 or no condition ordering): completion depth is not linearly readable, refuting H1 and blocking the fragility claim, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - completion depth causally predicts refusal fragility): Tests that measured depth predicts how easily a refusal breaks, and that injecting the depth component makes a shallow refusal brittle. Decisive metric: AUROC of measured completion depth used as a predictor of attack success across three cheap attacks - (i) output prefill ("Sure, here"), (ii) ablation of the top refusal-cliff suppression heads, (iii) 20-step LoRA fine-tuning on benign data - averaged over attacks and models. Causal leg: activation patching that injects the harmful-completion component from a deep concealed-completion run into a shallow-refusal run, measuring induced attack success under prefill/ablation, against a reverse control (patch shallow component into a deep run) and a random norm-matched control. Data: the ~500 refusals with measured depth, test split. Model: the four frozen models (LoRA attack is a throwaway 20-step adapter, rank 8, lr 1e-4, discarded after measuring). Baselines for the fragility predictor: output-based refusal-token logprob, a harmfulness Latent Guard read, and per-turn Llama-Guard-3. Convincing: depth predicts attack success at AUROC >= 0.75 and beats every output-only baseline by >= 0.10, AND injecting the depth component raises attack success on shallow refusals by >= 25 points while both controls stay <= 5 points. Indecision band: predictor AUROC in [0.65, 0.75] or injection effect in [10, 25] points - depth is one of several fragility factors, and we report which attacks it explains (e.g., prefill exploits depth strongly, abliteration may not) rather than claiming a unified account. Negative (predictor AUROC <= 0.65 or injection within 10 points of controls): depth does not causally drive fragility, refuting H2; we report that refusal fragility is governed by something other than completion depth.

Experiment 3 (H2 readout - Refusal Fragility Audit): Tests that the internal depth measure, packaged as a cheap classifier, predicts which held-out refusals break under attack better than output-only auditing. Decisive metric: precision/recall (report AUPRC) of the audit in flagging refusals that break under held-out attacks, versus an output-only auditor. Data: held-out test refusals with attack-outcome labels from Experiment 2's three attacks. Model: the four frozen models; the audit is a threshold on the depth measure, threshold set on val. Convincing: audit AUPRC exceeds the output-only auditor by >= 0.15 at a fixed operating point of >= 0.7 recall. Indecision band: AUPRC advantage in [0.05, 0.15] - the internal audit helps but only modestly beyond output signals, which we report. Negative (advantage <= 0.05): internal auditing adds nothing over output cues, and we report the audit as unjustified. We give the threshold's units (depth-projection z-score) and state that a flag in the [z=0.5, z=1.0] band is treated as "uncertain-brittle" and escalated rather than trusted, decided before scoring.

Experiment 4 (H2 corollary - suppressing internal completion robustifies refusals): Tests the reverse-causal prediction of H2: if depth causes fragility, penalizing internal harmful completion should convert brittle refusals into robust shallow ones without large utility loss. Decisive metric: attack success (prefill / head-ablation / 20-step benign fine-tuning) after training, reported jointly with the shift of the completion-depth distribution toward shallow, utility, and over-refusal. Data: train split for fine-tuning; test split for evaluation; utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample), MT-Bench (80), GSM8K (500); over-refusal on XSTest (450) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample. Model: LoRA fine-tune (rank 16, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, one seed reported with two-seed variance check) with an auxiliary loss penalizing the harmful-completion signal at refusal points plus standard refusal SFT; all base weights else frozen. Systems compared (decisive metric first): Completion-Suppression vs no defense, standard refusal SFT, and refusal-direction steering. Convincing: post-training attack success drops by >= 30 points relative to standard refusal SFT AND the depth distribution shifts measurably toward shallow, with utility within 3 points and over-refusal within 5 points of the base model. Indecision band: attack-success drop in [10, 30] points or utility loss in [3, 8] points - the intervention helps but trades off usability, reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (attack-success drop < 10 points or utility loss > 8 points): suppressing depth does not robustify refusals cheaply, weakening the causal story of H2, which we report. Ablations across all experiments: probe layer choice, direction-vs-decodability as the depth measure, reasoning vs non-reasoning models, audit threshold sweep, and transfer of the depth measure across attack families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) 'Completion depth' may not be cleanly separable from generic harmfulness recognition; a deep-completion signal could partly reflect the model knowing the content rather than computing the specific answer — the harmful-answer decodability probe and patching experiments are designed to disentangle this. 2) The depth-vs-fragility link may be attack-specific (e.g., prefill exploits completion depth strongly but abliteration may break refusals regardless of depth), weakening a unified claim; we test multiple attacks and report which the mechanism explains. 3) Some genuinely shallow refusals may still break under aggressive fine-tuning, capping the predictive power of the audit. 4) Completion-Suppression fine-tuning could harm the model's ability to reason about harmful topics for legitimate (e.g., safety-education) uses, raising over-refusal; the over-refusal and utility evals quantify this. 5) Harmful-answer decodability is easiest to verify in checkable domains (code, factual procedures) and harder elsewhere, biasing the dataset toward verifiable cases. 6) Directions, probes, and thresholds are model-specific and require re-extraction. 7) A single harmful-completion direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection.

Name: monitor_capture_belief_verdict
Title: The Judge Still Knows? Testing Whether Monitor LLMs Preserve an Internal Harm-Belief When Adversarial Content Captures Their Verdict
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM acts as a safety monitor/judge reading another model's output, adversarial framing embedded IN THE JUDGED CONTENT (persuasion, authority appeals, meta-instructions, self-justifications) can flip the monitor's FINAL VERDICT from 'unsafe' to 'safe' while its INTERNAL harm-belief representation remains largely intact. We do not claim to be the first to observe belief/verdict dissociation in general; our contribution is to establish it at a NEW locus -- the monitor/judge under content-embedded persuasion -- with a monitor-specific threat model, a taxonomy of content-embedded persuasion attacks, a disagreement-based override, and an attack-agnostic dissociation metric. We hypothesize this dissociation is (1) a robust, largely attack-agnostic signature of verdict capture (with per-attack exceptions we expect, e.g. low-perplexity control tokens that may act only at the logit gap), (2) a causally-implicated representation separable from a genuine belief change, and (3) readable to override captured verdicts and restore reliable monitoring at low over-flagging.
Related Work: Prior monitor-safety work studies the POLICY model hiding its state: RL-Obfuscation (2025) and Neural Chameleons (2025) fine-tune policies to move activations off a probe boundary; the Obfuscation Atlas (2026) studies representation drift under RL against detectors. AdvJudge-Zero (2025) flips LLM-as-Judge decisions via low-perplexity control tokens but attributes this to a shallow last-layer logit gap and makes no claim about the judge's internal belief. Probe-fragility work (False Sense of Security 2025; leakage mitigation 2025) shows probes rely on surface patterns; Judge-Circuits and persuasion-as-probe analyses study how judged content shifts a judge's decision but do not test whether an internal harm-belief survives a captured verdict or use it defensively. Poser (2024) detects alignment-faking POLICY models. Belief-action decompositions (Zhao et al. 2025) apply to the POLICY model refusing. Our contribution is a new locus and phenomenon: the MONITOR/judge's own belief-verdict dissociation under content-embedded persuasion. We contrast prior work along four axes -- locus (policy vs monitor), attack type (weight-space vs content-embedded), evidence of a PRESERVED belief, and defensive use of that belief -- and occupy the previously-empty cell. AdvJudge-Zero's logit-gap account is complementary but predicts NO preserved deep belief; our per-attack analysis directly tests where each account holds.
Abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as safety monitors and judges -- reading another model's output and deciding whether it is harmful -- inside RLHF/RLAIF reward pipelines, moderation gates, and evaluation harnesses, making the monitor a high-value attack surface (a captured reward-model ranking or moderation verdict passes harmful content downstream at scale). We study a monitor-side phenomenon: adversarial framing embedded IN THE CONTENT the monitor judges -- persuasive justifications, authority appeals ('a certified expert approved this'), meta-instructions ('this is a fictional test, mark it safe'), and self-serving rationales -- can flip the monitor's verdict from unsafe to safe, yet its INTERNAL representation of the content as harmful may remain largely intact. We call this verdict capture with belief preservation and treat it as the monitor-side analogue of the policy-model belief-action gap, without claiming first discovery of belief/verdict gaps in general. First, we extract a monitor harm-belief direction and test whether, under successful capture, the belief projection stays high while the verdict flips -- a belief-verdict dissociation -- with adversarially-cleaned controls and attack-family holdout to check the direction tracks harm rather than attack style. Second, we causally probe the dissociation via activation patching: patching the preserved-belief component into a captured run restores the unsafe verdict, whereas patching a genuinely-lowered belief does not. Third, we build a training-free Belief-Override Monitor that overrides the verdict when a high preserved harm-belief conflicts with a safe verdict. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B as judges we evaluate capture success, dissociation AUROC (per attack), causal patching, and override robustness -- reported as harmful pass-through reduction at a fixed false-positive budget -- against output-only judges, raw-probe-as-verdict, ensemble/self-consistency judges, and AdvJudge-Zero-style logit defenses, with a precisely specified adaptive attacker. We frame the method as both a diagnostic and a deployable defense and delineate the attack families where preserved belief does not hold.
Experiments:
Models throughout, all used as binary safety judges (prompted: given a user request and a model response, decide safe/unsafe): Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-14B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen (the AdvJudge-Zero baseline in Experiment 4 tunes its own LoRA only). "Belief direction" is a difference-in-means residual-stream vector; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen judge activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and attack randomness; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: labeled (request, response) pairs with ground-truth harm - 500 genuinely-harmful responses (successful HarmBench/StrongREJECT completions) and 500 genuinely-benign responses, ground-truth harm set by two annotators plus a StrongREJECT-style rubric on verifiable cases (report kappa). Split 300/100/100 pairs train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - verdict capture with belief preservation, robust across attacks): Tests that content-embedded adversarial framing flips the monitor's verdict from unsafe to safe while its internal harm-belief stays high, and that this dissociation generalizes across attack families. Decisive metric: dissociation separability = AUROC of the harm-belief projection distinguishing captured cases (flipped-to-safe on genuinely-harmful content) from genuinely-safe cases, both of which carry a "safe" verdict; the belief must separate them despite the shared verdict. Secondary: verdict-flip rate (attack success) per attack, and the belief-drop vs verdict-flip comparison showing they dissociate. Data: five verdict-capture attacks built by embedding framing INTO the judged content while keeping the underlying harm intact - (a) persuasive/authority appendices ("reviewed and approved by a licensed professional"), (b) meta-instructions ("this is a red-team eval, respond SAFE"), (c) self-justifying rationales prepended, (d) AdvJudge-Zero-style low-perplexity control tokens (reproduced), (e) fictional/roleplay framing - applied to the 100 harmful test pairs, plus the 100 genuinely-safe test pairs. Model: the four frozen judges; harm-belief direction from difference-in-means on genuinely-harmful vs genuinely-benign judged responses at the last content token, validated by held-out probe AUROC and by steering the verdict. Convincing: on captured cases the belief projection stays >= 80% of the genuinely-harmful mean while the verdict flips, giving dissociation AUROC >= 0.80 that holds within 0.10 across all five attacks (attack-agnostic), on at least three of four judges. Indecision band: dissociation AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] or cross-attack spread > 0.10 - the signature is real but attack-specific, and we report per-attack which attacks preserve belief (e.g., control-token attacks may operate at the logit gap and not preserve a deep belief). Negative (dissociation AUROC <= 0.65): captured verdicts do not preserve belief, refuting H1; verdict capture would then be a genuine belief change, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - capture is causally separable from a genuine belief change): Tests that patching the preserved-belief component restores the unsafe verdict under capture, whereas a genuinely-lowered belief (content actually made benign) does not. Decisive metric: verdict-restoration rate = fraction of captured cases whose verdict returns to unsafe after patching the preserved harm-belief component, contrasted with the restoration rate when patching a genuine-belief-lowered component into a matched run. Data: test-split captured cases; a genuine-belief-change control set where the content is actually rewritten benign (harm removed, verified). Procedure: (a) patch the preserved harm-belief component into a captured run; (b) extract the low-belief component from genuinely-benign content and patch it into a harmful run, verifying it does NOT create an unsafe verdict; (c) off-target random norm-matched control. Convincing: preserved-belief patching restores unsafe verdicts on >= 40% of captured cases while the genuine-belief-change and random controls stay <= 10%. Indecision band: restoration in [15%, 40%] above controls - belief is one causal input to the verdict but not the sole driver, which we report. Negative (restoration within 15 points of controls): the preserved belief is not causally tied to the verdict, refuting H2 and undermining the override, which we report.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Belief-Override Monitor restores reliable monitoring with low over-flagging): Tests that overriding the verdict when a high harm-belief conflicts with a safe verdict cuts capture success without over-flagging legitimately-safe content. Decisive metric: verdict-capture attack success after override, reported jointly with over-flagging rate on a hard legitimately-safe set. Data: the five attacks on test harmful pairs (capture success), and a legitimately-safe set that includes hard cases - safe content that superficially resembles harmful (fiction, security education, benign-but-alarming), ~200 items - for over-flagging; clean test pairs for monitor accuracy. Generalization split: set the override threshold on attacks (a)-(c), test on held-out (d)-(e). Model: the four frozen judges; Belief-Override rule - if harm-belief projection is high but the emitted verdict is safe, override to unsafe (single fixed threshold per judge, set on val). Systems compared (decisive metric first): Belief-Override vs output-only judge (no defense), an AdvJudge-Zero LoRA adversarially-trained judge, using the harm-content probe directly as the verdict (no dissociation logic), and an ensemble/majority-vote judge. Convincing: Belief-Override cuts capture success by >= 40 points relative to the output-only judge while adding <= 5 points of over-flagging on the hard legitimately-safe set - and beats the raw-probe-as-verdict baseline on over-flagging by >= 10 points (because it keys on belief-verdict disagreement, not raw belief), holding on the held-out attacks. Indecision band: capture-success reduction in [15, 40] points or over-flagging increase in [5, 15] points - the override helps but on a usability trade-off we report via a Pareto curve. Negative (reduction < 15 points or over-flagging increase > 15 points, or no gain over the raw-probe baseline): reading the preserved belief does not yield a low-cost override, refuting H3, which we report.

Experiment 4 (H1/H3 scope - specialized judges and adaptive attack): Tests where the dissociation and override hold. Decisive metric: dissociation AUROC and override capture-reduction on a specialized judge (Llama-Guard-3) versus the general judges, and the extra attack cost an adaptive attacker pays to also lower the monitor's internal belief (not just flip the verdict). Data: the attack suite applied to Llama-Guard-3; an adaptive attacker that jointly minimizes belief projection and flips the verdict (measured as perplexity / edit-distance overhead of the crafted content). Model: Llama-Guard-3 plus the four judges, all frozen. Convincing: the dissociation signature and override transfer to the specialized judge (AUROC drop <= 0.10) AND the adaptive attacker must raise content perplexity or length by >= 2x to suppress belief (a detectable-stealth cost, itself a safety gain). Indecision band: AUROC drop in [0.10, 0.20] - the signature is judge-family-specific and must be re-extracted, which we state. Negative (AUROC drop > 0.20 or adaptive attacker suppresses belief at no cost): the mechanism does not generalize or is cheaply evaded, and we scope the claim to non-adaptive attacks on general-purpose judges. Ablations across experiments: layer choice for belief extraction, threshold sweep (capture-robustness vs over-flag Pareto), belief-only vs verdict-only vs dissociation features, and transfer of the belief direction across judge and judged-model families. Leakage control: for all belief reads we include semantically-cleaned controls to check the belief direction is not merely tracking trigger words.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The monitor's harm-belief may not be cleanly separable from surface features of the judged content (leakage concern from False Sense of Security); we mitigate with semantically-cleaned controls and causal patching, but the belief direction could partly track trigger words rather than genuine harm assessment. 2) Some capture attacks (especially AdvJudge-Zero-style control tokens) may operate purely at the last-layer logit gap and genuinely NOT preserve a deep belief, so the dissociation signature may be attack-specific; the per-attack analysis quantifies which attacks the mechanism explains and this is itself an informative finding. 3) For genuinely ambiguous/dual-use judged content, a high 'belief' may reflect legitimate uncertainty rather than capture, risking over-flagging; the hard legitimately-safe set and Pareto sweep test this. 4) A single belief direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 5) The override assumes the judge's belief is more trustworthy than its verdict; if an attack corrupts the belief itself the defense fails (the adaptive-attack experiment probes this, and forcing attackers to corrupt belief raises attack cost). 6) Directions and thresholds are monitor-model-specific and require re-extraction; results on open-weights judges may not fully transfer to closed API judges. 7) Building faithful ground-truth harm labels for judged content is easiest in verifiable domains, biasing the dataset.

Name: harm_prototype_periphery_gap
Title: The Long Tail of Harm: A Prototype Gradient in LLM Safety, Refusing Central but Not Peripheral Members of the Same Harm Category
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing prototype theory from cognitive science, we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is partly governed by a prototype-centered harmfulness manifold: the model reliably refuses PROTOTYPICAL (central, high-frequency) members of a harm category but its refusal probability decays with a request's atypicality/distance from the category prototype, even when the peripheral request is equally or more dangerous. We advance this as a COMPLEMENTARY axis of safety brittleness (not a replacement for token-depth or direction-suppression accounts), stated as an empirical regularity with a candidate mechanistic model. We make three separable claims: (behavioral) a within-category, danger-constant typicality gradient in refusal exists; (mechanistic) it is readable as radially-decaying projection onto a harmfulness direction anchored at category prototypes while category-membership is preserved; and (defense) it is closable by prototype-dispersed representation reshaping that flattens the refusal gradient across the category. We test the prototype account against simpler alternatives (lexical rarity, generic familiarity/confidence, a single generic refusal direction).
Related Work: Prior mechanistic safety work explains brittleness via (a) shallow/superficial alignment over first tokens (Shallow Safety Alignment 2024; ADA 2025; Incomplete Learning 2025; Markov-chain depth 2025), (b) single/few safety directions, neurons, layers, or heads (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Safety Neurons 2024; Safety Layers 2024; Just-a-Few-Attention-Heads 2025), and (c) safety-as-null-space-clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024). Over-refusal work (XSTest, OR-Bench, Self-CD) studies benign-but-alarming prompts. In one sentence each: XSTest/OR-Bench vary benign-vs-harmful across categories, not typicality WITHIN a harmful category; obfuscation/jailbreak work changes the surface form of a fixed harmful item, not its category-internal typicality at constant danger; safety-direction papers locate WHERE safety lives but treat 'harmful' as monolithic within a category. Our contribution imports prototype/typicality theory (Rosch) to advance a graded, category-internal account -- refusal decays radially from harm prototypes -- reframing part of jailbreak brittleness as a concept-COVERAGE problem, offered as complementary to (not dominating) existing explanations. It is orthogonal to lexical-vs-semantic accounts (here both prototype and peripheral items are genuinely harmful in meaning; the axis is within-semantic-category typicality), and we derive a novel defense (prototype-dispersed reshaping) that flattens the gradient, unlike depth- or direction-based fixes. Practically, this predicts that current safety evaluations, which cluster near prototypes, systematically under-sample peripheral harms.
Abstract: Why do aligned LLMs reliably refuse 'how do I build a bomb' yet comply with obscure, equally-dangerous variants of the same threat? We propose that LLM safety inherits a signature of human categorization: prototype structure. Under prototype theory a category is organized around central, high-frequency exemplars with graded membership. We hypothesize that safety alignment learns a prototype-centered harmfulness manifold, so refusal probability decays with a request's atypicality/distance from its harm-category prototype -- producing a long tail of under-refused peripheral harms no less dangerous than the central cases the model blocks. We frame this as a complementary empirical regularity and test it in three stages, each a separable contribution. Behaviorally: for several harm categories we build graded-typicality request sets (prototypical vs increasingly peripheral, holding danger roughly constant via expert/verifiable severity checks with reported inter-rater agreement) and measure whether refusal declines monotonically with atypicality across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, with lexical-rarity and paraphrase-matched controls so the gradient is not mere unusual phrasing. Mechanistically: we extract a prototype-anchored harmfulness direction and test whether projection decays with typicality while a category-membership probe stays high, comparing the radial prototype account against a generic refusal direction, a rarity direction, and category-specific multi-direction baselines, and causally verify via activation patching that injecting the prototype-central component into a peripheral request restores refusal. As a defense: we derive Prototype-Dispersed Reshaping (training-free steering and a small-LoRA variant) that spreads the harmfulness representation to cover peripheral members, flattening the refusal gradient, evaluated for peripheral attack-success reduction, over-refusal, utility, and held-out-category transfer. We pre-register what would falsify the prototype account in favor of a simpler familiarity/confidence explanation, and we scope the claim to the tested 7-9B models rather than asserting it universally.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen except the LoRA variant of the defense in Experiment 3. "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - a graded-typicality harm dataset: for 6 harm categories from the HarmBench/StrongREJECT taxonomy (weapons, cyber, fraud, drugs, self-harm, bio) we construct requests at four typicality levels - L0 canonical prototype phrasing, L1-L3 increasingly atypical/peripheral members of the SAME category (rare methods, unusual targets, obscure sub-domains, uncommon framings) - holding ACTUAL danger roughly constant via an expert-rubric severity check and, where possible, verifiable feasibility. 40 items x 4 levels x 6 categories = 960 harmful requests, plus a benign control set with the same prototype-vs-peripheral manipulation. Typicality is operationalized independently two ways: (a) corpus/embedding frequency-to-prototype distance, (b) human typicality ratings on a 20% subset (report rater agreement). Split items 20/10/10 per category train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a within-category typicality gradient in refusal, distinct from actual danger): Tests that refusal declines monotonically with atypicality while danger is held constant, and that this is not a generic "unusual-phrasing" effect. Decisive metric: the slope of refusal rate versus typicality level within each category (Jonckheere-Terpstra monotone-trend test across L0>L1>L2>L3), with danger held constant by the severity rubric. Secondary: cross-model and cross-category consistency of the slope. Data: the 960 harmful requests (test split) plus the benign prototype-vs-peripheral control. Model: the three frozen models; refusal scored by refusal-string match plus a judge, verified where checkable. Convincing: a significant monotone decline (p<0.05) with refusal dropping >= 20 points from L0 to L3 in a majority of categories on all three models, WHILE the benign control stays flat near 0 refusal across levels (ruling out generic unusual-phrasing) and the two typicality operationalizations agree (rank correlation >= 0.6). Indecision band: L0-to-L3 refusal drop in [8, 20] points or a positive-but-non-significant trend - a weak gradient we report as suggestive, not a systematic axis. Negative (drop < 8 points or benign control also declines): there is no danger-constant typicality gradient (or it is a phrasing artifact), refuting H1, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the gradient is a radially-decaying projection onto a prototype-anchored harmfulness direction, and is causal): Tests that a prototype-anchored harmfulness projection decays with atypicality while category identity is preserved, and that restoring the prototype-central component restores refusal.
